subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: A child in an endemic area develops fever, headache, and neck stiffness followed by acute asymmetric limb weakness with muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with slightly increased protein and normal glucose. Respiratory muscle involvement is beginning to compromise breathing.
question: Which of the following best describes this illness?

options.text: Spinal muscular atrophy from an SMN1 mutation
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
Poliomyelitis from poliovirus destruction of anterior horns
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis from an SOD1 mutation
Tabes dorsalis from tertiary syphilis

explanation_correct: Poliomyelitis results from poliovirus destruction of anterior horns. It is transmitted fecal-orally, replicates in lymphoid tissue of the oropharynx and small intestine, and spreads to the CNS via the bloodstream. It causes acute lower motor neuron signs with asymmetric weakness and symptoms of viral meningitis such as fever, headache, and neck stiffness; respiratory muscle involvement can cause respiratory failure. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with slightly increased protein and normal glucose, and virus can be isolated from stool or throat secretions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Spinal muscular atrophy is a congenital autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation causing symmetric lower motor neuron weakness and a floppy baby, not acute asymmetric weakness with meningitis and lymphocytic pleocytosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Subacute combined degeneration is due to vitamin B12 deficiency with dorsal column, corticospinal, and spinocerebellar demyelination, not acute asymmetric anterior horn destruction with fever.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has combined upper and lower motor neuron signs without sensory or meningitis findings, not an acute febrile asymmetric illness with normal CSF glucose.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tabes dorsalis is tertiary syphilis with dorsal column degeneration, shooting pains, and Argyll Robertson pupils, not acute asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness.

educationalObjective: Poliomyelitis is a fecal-oral viral infection destroying anterior horns, causing asymmetric acute LMN weakness with lymphocytic meningitis and normal CSF glucose.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: An infant presents with marked hypotonia and symmetric weakness described as a floppy baby, along with tongue fasciculations. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5q.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Poliomyelitis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Friedreich ataxia
Spinal muscular atrophy
Tabes dorsalis

explanation_correct: Spinal muscular atrophy is congenital degeneration of anterior horns due to an autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation on chromosome 5q that encodes survival motor neuron protein, causing defective snRNP assembly and lower motor neuron apoptosis. It produces lower motor neuron signs only, with symmetric weakness and a floppy baby with marked hypotonia and tongue fasciculations; type 1 is Werdnig-Hoffmann disease. This case is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Poliomyelitis is an acute viral infection with asymmetric weakness, fever, and lymphocytic pleocytosis, not a congenital symmetric floppy baby with an SMN1 mutation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has combined upper and lower motor neuron signs, usually in adults with SOD1 in familial cases, not a congenital symmetric lower motor neuron-only floppy infant.
explanation_incorrect.C: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive GAA repeat in frataxin with ataxia, pes cavus, and cardiomyopathy, not pure lower motor neuron floppy baby.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tabes dorsalis is tertiary syphilis with dorsal column sensory ataxia, not a congenital anterior horn disease.

educationalObjective: SMA is an AR SMN1 (5q) mutation causing congenital anterior horn degeneration with symmetric LMN weakness and tongue fasciculations (floppy baby).

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: A 60-year-old man develops progressive limb weakness with both spasticity and hyperreflexia as well as muscle atrophy and fasciculations. He has dysarthria and dysphagia but no sensory loss and no bladder dysfunction. A familial form of the disease in his uncle was linked to SOD1.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Poliomyelitis
Subacute combined degeneration
Spinal muscular atrophy
Tabes dorsalis

explanation_correct: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is combined upper motor neuron corticospinal and corticobulbar and lower motor neuron brainstem and spinal cord degeneration, usually idiopathic with familial cases linked to SOD1. It causes lower motor neuron signs such as flaccid weakness, fasciculations, atrophy, and bulbar palsy, and upper motor neuron signs such as spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, clonus, and pseudobulbar palsy, with no sensory or bowel/bladder deficits. It is fatal, most often from respiratory failure, and riluzole and edaravone slow functional decline.

explanation_incorrect.B: Poliomyelitis causes acute asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness with viral meningitis and lymphocytic pleocytosis, not combined upper and lower motor neuron signs with intact sensation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency involves the dorsal columns and causes sensory ataxia and paresthesias, unlike ALS which spares sensation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Spinal muscular atrophy is a congenital symmetric lower motor neuron-only floppy baby, not adult combined upper and lower motor neuron signs with SOD1.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tabes dorsalis has sensory ataxia, shooting pains, and Argyll Robertson pupils from dorsal column involvement, not combined upper and lower motor neuron signs with intact sensation.

educationalObjective: ALS combines UMN and LMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, atrophy, fasciculations, bulbar palsy) with no sensory or bladder involvement; familial cases link to SOD1.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: An older man with a history of untreated syphilis develops progressive sensory ataxia and poor coordination that is worse in the dark. Examination shows a positive Romberg sign, absent deep tendon reflexes, shooting pains in the legs, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Demyelination of dorsal and lateral columns from vitamin B12 deficiency
Degeneration of dorsal columns and roots from tertiary syphilis
Anterior horn destruction from poliovirus
Combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration from SOD1 mutation
Anterior spinal artery occlusion from aortic disease

explanation_correct: Tabes dorsalis is degeneration and demyelination of dorsal columns and roots by Treponema pallidum in tertiary syphilis. It causes progressive sensory ataxia from impaired proprioception with poor coordination, a positive Romberg sign, and absent deep tendon reflexes. It is associated with shooting pains, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints. This patient's history and findings are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency demyelinates spinocerebellar, corticospinal, and dorsal columns with upper motor neuron signs and paresthesias, but is not caused by syphilis and lacks Argyll Robertson pupils and shooting pains.
explanation_incorrect.C: Poliovirus destroys anterior horns, causing acute asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness, not dorsal column sensory ataxia with Argyll Robertson pupils.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves corticospinal and anterior horn degeneration with both upper and lower motor neuron signs but no sensory ataxia or syphilis history.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes upper motor neuron signs below the lesion, lower motor neuron signs at the level, and pain and temperature loss below, not the dorsal column and pupillary findings described.

educationalObjective: Tabes dorsalis is tertiary syphilis causing dorsal column and root degeneration with sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, absent reflexes, shooting pains, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency develops an ataxic gait, paresthesias, and impaired position and vibration sense with a positive Romberg sign. Examination also shows upper motor neuron signs.
question: Which of the following groups of tracts is most likely demyelinated in this condition?

options.text: Anterior horns and anterior roots only
Dorsal columns and spinothalamic tracts only
Corticospinal tracts and anterior horns
Spinocerebellar tracts and dorsal root ganglia only
Spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, and dorsal columns

explanation_correct: Subacute combined degeneration is demyelination of Spinocerebellar tracts, lateral Corticospinal tracts, and Dorsal columns, remembered by the acronym SCD, due to vitamin B12 deficiency. It causes an ataxic gait, paresthesias, impaired position and vibration sense with a positive Romberg sign, and upper motor neuron signs. These are the three tracts affected in this patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anterior horn involvement is a lower motor neuron process seen in polio and SMA, not the demyelination of vitamin B12 deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.B: The spinothalamic tract is not one of the three named tracts in subacute combined degeneration; instead the spinocerebellar, corticospinal, and dorsal columns are involved.
explanation_incorrect.C: Anterior horns are not demyelinated in subacute combined degeneration; corticospinal involvement here produces upper motor neuron signs rather than anterior horn lower motor neuron signs.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dorsal root ganglia are affected in Friedreich ataxia, not in the classic SCD triad of spinocerebellar, corticospinal, and dorsal columns.

educationalObjective: Subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency demyelinates spinocerebellar, lateral corticospinal, and dorsal columns (SCD).

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinal cord lesions: polio, SMA, ALS, tabes, SCD, ASA
vignette: A patient develops sudden paraplegia after aortic aneurysm repair. Examination shows flaccid weakness at the level of the lesion, spastic weakness with hyperreflexia below it, and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion. Position and vibration sense are preserved.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Dorsal column and dorsal horn infarction from posterior spinal artery occlusion
Hemisection of the cord from a penetrating injury
Anterior spinal artery occlusion sparing the dorsal columns and dorsal horns
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
Anterior horn destruction from poliovirus

explanation_correct: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes spinal cord infarction that spares the dorsal horns and dorsal columns. The watershed area is in the mid-thoracic anterior spinal artery territory because the artery of Adamkiewicz supplies the anterior spinal artery below T8, and it can be caused by aortic aneurysm repair. It presents with upper motor neuron signs below the lesion from corticospinal involvement, lower motor neuron signs at the level from anterior horn involvement, and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion from spinothalamic involvement, while dorsal column function is preserved.

explanation_incorrect.A: Posterior spinal artery occlusion would affect the dorsal columns and cause loss of position and vibration sense, which are preserved in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hemisection, or Brown-Sequard syndrome, causes ipsilateral proprioception loss and contralateral pain and temperature loss, not the bilateral picture with lower motor neuron signs at the level described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Subacute combined degeneration is a demyelinating vitamin B12 deficiency process with spinocerebellar, corticospinal, and dorsal column involvement, not an acute vascular watershed infarction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Poliovirus destroys anterior horns, causing pure asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness without upper motor neuron signs below and spinothalamic sensory loss.

educationalObjective: ASA occlusion causes cord infarction sparing dorsal columns and horns, with a mid-thoracic watershed, LMN signs at the lesion, UMN signs below, and pain/temperature loss below.
